strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates the limitation of static full-series encoding and proposes adaptive segment selection as a natural solution
Technically sound hierarchical RL approach with asymmetric optimization for controller (trajectory-level) and reasoner (final-round), well-justified for the task structure
Comprehensive evaluation across six diverse benchmarks (clinical, financial, environmental, general) with broad baseline coverage (text LLMs, domain-specific, vision-language models)
Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) demonstrating each component's contribution; reliability reward shows 21.44% impact when removed
Insightful data utilization analysis (Figure 3) showing accuracy peaks at 30-70% coverage, providing evidence for selective processing benefit
Extensive reproducibility details: prompts, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and SFT curation procedures in appendices
Clever reliability-based reward (Eq. 8) using answer consistency under repeated sampling to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky correct outputs
weaknesses: Unclear necessity of adaptive selection: Figure 3 doesn't prove that adaptive (reasoning-based) selection outperforms static segment sampling at 30-70% coverage; simpler approaches may achieve similar results

Imbalanced contribution: SFT alone provides 5.65 average accuracy points (~75% of total 6.46 gain), while RL adds only 1.81 points, raising questions about whether RL's adaptive selection is the primary driver

Anomalous Sleep-QA results: ARTIST achieves only 36.63% vs. TimeMaster+RL's 72.55% (36-point gap), suggesting approach may fail on biomedical signals; this critical finding receives insufficient analysis
Limited technical scope: restricted to univariate time series, contiguous segments only (no multi-span), and max 3 segment selections; constraint justifications not provided

Inference cost not quantified: paper acknowledges 'additional inference cost' but provides no latency measurements, number of typical segment selections, or cost-benefit analysis critical for practitioners
Hyperparameter choices unjustified: controller/reasoner temperatures (1.0/0.7), LoRA rank, learning rate (1×10⁻⁶) lack ablations or justification
Reliability reward dependency on LLM stochasticity: approach critically depends on temperature-based variance (Eq. 8); generalization to deterministic models or different architectures unexplored
Missing statistical significance testing: while 8 runs reported, no confidence intervals or tests; is 6.46% improvement statistically robust?
Insufficient error analysis: no breakdown of which question types benefit from adaptive selection, failure mode analysis beyond one example, or investigation of anomalous results

strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying a genuine gap in time series reasoning: most prior work encodes full series upfront despite question-dependent segment relevance
Solid technical approach with controller-reasoner decomposition that meaningfully separates segment selection from reasoning, plus hierarchical RL with appropriate credit assignment across rounds
Clever use of reliability rewards (Eq. 8) to handle LLM stochasticity via consistency across rollouts, and variance-guided sampling (Eq. 12) for informative segment prioritization
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks with strong empirical results: 6.46% average accuracy improvement with up to 12.5% gains on rare event/multi-segment tasks
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of key components: adaptive selection (-9.30%), reliability reward (-21.44%), hierarchical optimization (-12.28%)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, training costs, dataset descriptions, and supplementary analyses of data utilization patterns and long-sequence generalization
Well-written paper with clear motivation, accessible technical presentation, and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Substantial inference cost of 1.6-2.1× per example compared to baselines (Table 8) is relegated to Appendix I despite being a significant practical limitation for deployment
Inconsistent performance across datasets: Sleep-QA (36.63%) substantially underperforms TimeMaster+RL (72.55%), indicating modality/representation sensitivities not fully addressed in main approach

Limited technical novelty—builds incrementally on recent self-play RL work (AZR, SPICE, SPELL); controller-reasoner decomposition is sensible but not novel; reliability rewards are straightforward accuracy averaging

Evaluation fairness concerns: uneven SFT treatment across baselines, no statistical significance tests, some improvements modest (1-3%) without confidence intervals, comparison sometimes mixes method and representation effects

Restricted scope: univariate only, most benchmarks are short (22-4,000 tokens), long-sequence experiments use artificial setup (tiling + noise rather than realistic long series), no multivariate evaluation

SFT data introduces circularity: GPT-5 creates gold standard traces then ARTIST fine-tunes on them; ablation shows SFT gain (+5.65%) substantially exceeds RL gain (+0.81%), raising attribution questions

Design choices under-justified: different controller/reasoner temperatures (1.0 vs 0.7) mentioned only in appendix, format reward penalties appear ad-hoc, missing ablations on format rewards and interaction round limits

Incomplete analysis: only 3 qualitative examples (Figure 4), no systematic study of failure modes, missing analysis of how questions yield different segment selections, limited comparison with PixelReasoner (Table 7, single dataset)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine limitation in time-series reasoning—adaptive segment selection during inference is intuitive and practical
Technically sound controller-reasoner decomposition with sensible hierarchical RL optimization that provides trajectory-level supervision for the controller
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six diverse benchmarks with thorough ablation studies and multiple baseline types (LLMs, fine-tuned encoders, vision models)
Strong empirical results with 6.46% average accuracy improvement and up to 12.5 points on targeted reasoning tasks
Extensive reproducibility details including hyperparameters, training costs, and detailed prompts in appendices
Insightful data utilization analysis showing the model selectively uses 30-70% of input, validating the selective reasoning hypothesis
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation inadequately addressed: inference is 1.3-2.6× slower than baselines (1.68-2.08 min vs 0.78-1.29 min per example), undermining efficiency claims for long sequences. This overhead deserves prominence equal to accuracy improvements, especially given modest gains on some datasets (1.26 points on Sleep-QA)

Limited technical novelty—controller-reasoner architecture, reliability-based rewards via sampling, and hierarchical RL are largely existing techniques. The contribution is primarily their combination, which is incremental

Restricted scope to univariate time series (V=1) significantly limits real-world applicability (e.g., clinical vital signs, financial portfolios are multivariate). Extension to multivariate is deferred to future work

Reproducibility barrier: SFT reasoning traces generated using GPT-5 + post-processing, making results dependent on proprietary model. No analysis of how SFT data quality impacts downstream performance. Unreproducible without GPT-5 access

Lack of statistical rigor: 8 runs reported but no significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values. No assessment of whether improvements (especially 1.26% on Sleep-QA) are statistically significant. Small test sets (200-226 samples) increase variance

Modality sensitivity undermines generalizability: Appendix G shows ARTIST+VLM backbone achieves 65% vs 28% for tokenized input on Sleep-QA, suggesting segment selection mechanism is fragile and heavily input-representation dependent rather than fundamentally improving reasoning

Segment selection evaluation is indirect—paper measures answer correctness but not segment informativeness. No ground-truth segment annotations exist. Unclear whether selected segments are genuinely informative beyond final accuracy

Massive computational requirements limit reproducibility: RL stage requires 4 H100 GPUs for 23-27 hours, training only 1 epoch. Improvement of 5.65%→6.46% is modest relative to compute cost. The 1.3-2.6× inference overhead further limits practical utility
Critical hyperparameter choices left unjustified: G=6, N=6, temperatures chosen without sensitivity analysis. No ablation on these values or justification for why alternatives weren't tried
Incomplete baseline analysis: Some baselines achieve 0.00 accuracy on RCW (e.g., Qwen3-8B), raising questions about proper configuration. Limited analysis of why certain models fail so dramatically
No direct failure case analysis—only cherry-picked successful examples shown. Unknown when segment selection helps vs. hurts, or what question types challenge the approach

Reliability reward (Eq. 8) design concerns: Measures consistency without distinguishing 'consistently correct' from 'consistently wrong', potentially incentivizing overly conservative selections. Sensitivity to N not analyzed
Format rewards appear ad-hoc without justification for penalty values or ablation studies specifically examining these components

Segment selection mechanism unclear—no explicit attention or proposal mechanism; relies entirely on learned behavior from SFT. Risk of overfitting to SFT data distribution. No defense against degenerate solutions

Scalability analysis (Appendix J) uses only synthetic extended-length data created by tiling + noise. Real distributional shift not evaluated. Unclear if controller generalizes to substantially different sequence structures

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to address question-adaptive segment selection in time-series reasoning, with clear distinction from vision-language search due to context-dependent, non-isolated temporal segments

Well-justified hierarchical architecture: Controller-reasoner decomposition enables role-specific learning signals (trajectory-level vs. final-round optimization) that is more principled than myopic self-play approaches

Comprehensive experimental validation: Six diverse benchmarks across clinical, financial, environmental domains; consistent 6.46% average improvement with detailed ablations demonstrating necessity of each component
Strong evidence for core hypothesis: Figure 3 shows optimal utilization at 30-70% of data; >90% reduces performance, validating selective analysis approach
Thorough reproducibility support: Detailed hyperparameters, training costs (~104 GPU-hours), SFT data curation process, prompts, and implementation details in appendices
Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges inference cost (1.6-2.6× overhead) and univariate-only scope upfront
weaknesses: Substantial inference cost: 1.68-2.08 minutes per example vs. 0.78-1.29 for baselines limits practical applicability; needs deeper cost-benefit analysis for when overhead is justified
Limited to univariate signals: Only evaluated on single-variable time series; extension to multivariate data (multiple sensors/variables) non-trivial, reducing real-world applicability

Reliability reward design lacks rigorous justification: Uses N=6 rollouts with no sensitivity analysis; conflates segment quality with answer correctness; assumes consistency implies good segments, but could be confounded by question difficulty; variance-guided sampling motivation unclear
SFT data concerns: Uses GPT-5 as ground truth (may bias training), arbitrary constraints (3 segments max, 8 timesteps min), no analysis of synthetic trace quality or propagation of errors
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals or significance tests despite 8 runs; some improvements modest (e.g., +2.94 TRQA); unclear which differences are statistically significant

Baseline comparison issues: Text-based LLMs surprisingly weak (28-35% on most datasets), suggesting undertrained/misprompted models; comparing multi-pass method against single-pass baselines conflates design with compute

Limited failure analysis: Sleep-QA shows minimal improvement attributed to modality, but lacks deeper investigation; no analysis of which question types struggle or when adaptive selection hurts vs. helps
Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: Fixed temperatures (controller: 1.0, reasoner: 0.7), KL (β=0.002), LoRA rank (8); no ablations despite these being non-obvious choices

Scalability analysis limitations: Appendix J uses artificial setting where task-relevant regions [0,4000) remain unchanged in extended sequences; real long sequences with distributed relevant regions may behave differently
